<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<title>React Training — Interview Prep</title>
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Atkinson+Hyperlegible+Next:ital,wght@0,400;0,500;0,700;1,400&family=Bricolage+Grotesque:opsz,wght@12..96,500..800&family=IBM+Plex+Mono:wght@400;500;600&family=Caveat:wght@600;700&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
<style>
  /* study-theme v4 "whiteboard": the one stylesheet every guide uses. Edit here, then run
     `npm run study:upgrade` to apply it to every guide (lib.upgrade swaps each guide's <style> for this file).
     Token names are also used inside the SVG diagrams (dg*.mjs), so rename none of them. */
  :root{
    /* light: a whiteboard. Navy ink, blue marker for actions, green for done, yellow highlighter. */
    --bg:#F5F7FA;
    --panel:#FFFFFF;
    --panel-2:#EEF2F7;
    --border:#D3DAE5;
    --text:#14213D;
    --muted:#4F5D78;
    --accent:#1B55C5;
    --accent-ink:#FFFFFF;
    --accent-soft:#E4EDFC;
    --gold:#7A5200;
    --gold-soft:#FFF1B8;
    --ok:#126B4B;
    --ok-soft:#DDF3E9;
    --code-bg:#EEF2F7;
    --danger:#B42318;
    --shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(20,33,61,.06), 0 4px 14px rgba(20,33,61,.04);
    --mono: 'IBM Plex Mono', ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
    --sans: 'Atkinson Hyperlegible Next', 'Atkinson Hyperlegible', -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', sans-serif;
    --display: 'Bricolage Grotesque', var(--sans);
    --hand: 'Caveat', 'Segoe Print', 'Bradley Hand', 'Comic Sans MS', cursive;
    --measure: 76ch;
  }
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark){
    :root:not([data-theme="light"]){
      /* dark: a chalkboard. Chalk white text, chalk blue / yellow / green accents. */
      --bg:#101A19;
      --panel:#17231F;
      --panel-2:#1E2D29;
      --border:#33493F;
      --text:#ECF1EE;
      --muted:#A9B8B1;
      --accent:#93BCFF;
      --accent-ink:#0A1730;
      --accent-soft:#1D3048;
      --gold:#F0CF6B;
      --gold-soft:#3A3216;
      --ok:#7FD6A8;
      --ok-soft:#173327;
      --code-bg:#0C1513;
      --danger:#F5A99C;
      --shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.4);
    }
  }
  :root[data-theme="dark"]{
    --bg:#101A19;
    --panel:#17231F;
    --panel-2:#1E2D29;
    --border:#33493F;
    --text:#ECF1EE;
    --muted:#A9B8B1;
    --accent:#93BCFF;
    --accent-ink:#0A1730;
    --accent-soft:#1D3048;
    --gold:#F0CF6B;
    --gold-soft:#3A3216;
    --ok:#7FD6A8;
    --ok-soft:#173327;
    --code-bg:#0C1513;
    --danger:#F5A99C;
    --shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.4);
  }

  *{box-sizing:border-box;}
  html,body{margin:0;padding:0;}
  html{color-scheme:light dark; scroll-padding-top:16px;}
  body{
    background:var(--bg);
    color:var(--text);
    font-family:var(--sans);
    font-size:16px;
    line-height:1.6;
    -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased;
    text-rendering:optimizeLegibility;
  }
  a{color:var(--accent); text-underline-offset:2px;}
  :focus-visible{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:2px; border-radius:4px;}
  ::selection{background:var(--gold-soft); color:var(--text);}

  .app{display:flex; min-height:100vh;}

  /* ---------- Sidebar ---------- */
  .sidebar{
    width:288px;
    flex:0 0 288px;
    border-right:1px solid var(--border);
    background:var(--panel);
    padding:18px 14px 24px;
    position:sticky;
    top:0;
    height:100vh;
    overflow-y:auto;
    scrollbar-width:thin;
  }
  .side-top{display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between; gap:8px; margin:0 0 14px;}
  .home-link{display:inline-flex; align-items:center; gap:6px; font-size:14px; font-weight:500; color:var(--muted); text-decoration:none; padding:6px 8px; border-radius:8px;}
  .home-link:hover{color:var(--accent); background:var(--accent-soft);}
  .theme-btn{font:inherit; font-size:15px; line-height:1; width:34px; height:34px; color:var(--muted); background:transparent; border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:8px; cursor:pointer;}
  .theme-btn:hover{color:var(--accent); border-color:var(--accent);}
  .brand{
    font-size:13.5px;
    line-height:1.45;
    color:var(--muted);
    padding:0 8px 16px;
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--border);
    margin-bottom:14px;
  }
  .brand b{display:block; font-family:var(--display); font-size:19px; font-weight:700; letter-spacing:-0.01em; color:var(--text);}
  .brand br{display:none;}
  .nav-item{
    display:flex;
    align-items:center;
    justify-content:space-between;
    gap:10px;
    width:100%;
    text-align:left;
    padding:9px 10px;
    border-radius:9px;
    border:1px solid transparent;
    background:transparent;
    color:var(--text);
    font-family:var(--sans);
    font-size:15px;
    line-height:1.35;
    cursor:pointer;
    margin-bottom:2px;
  }
  .nav-item:hover{background:var(--panel-2);}
  .nav-item.active{background:var(--accent-soft); color:var(--text); font-weight:700; box-shadow:inset 3px 0 0 var(--accent);}
  .nav-num{font-size:12.5px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--muted); width:20px; flex:0 0 20px;}
  .nav-item.active .nav-num{color:var(--accent);}
  .nav-label{flex:1;}
  .nav-count{
    font-size:12px;
    font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;
    color:var(--muted);
    background:var(--panel-2);
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    padding:1px 7px;
    border-radius:999px;
  }
  .nav-item.complete .nav-count{color:var(--ok); border-color:var(--ok); background:var(--ok-soft);}
  .progress-box{
    margin-top:20px;
    padding:14px 12px;
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:12px;
    background:var(--panel-2);
  }
  .progress-box .label{font-size:12.5px; font-weight:700; color:var(--muted); margin-bottom:8px; text-transform:lowercase;}
  .progress-box .label::first-letter{text-transform:uppercase;}
  .progress-track{height:8px; border-radius:999px; background:var(--border); overflow:hidden;}
  .progress-fill{height:100%; background:var(--ok); width:0%; transition:width .25s ease;}
  .progress-num{margin-top:8px; font-size:13.5px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--text);}
  .reset-btn{
    margin-top:10px;
    width:100%;
    font-family:var(--sans);
    font-size:13px;
    color:var(--muted);
    background:transparent;
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:8px;
    padding:7px 8px;
    cursor:pointer;
  }
  .reset-btn:hover{color:var(--danger);border-color:var(--danger);}

  /* ---------- Main ---------- */
  .main{
    flex:1;
    min-width:0;
    padding:40px 48px 96px;
    max-width:1080px;
  }
  .hero{margin-bottom:36px;}
  .hero .eyebrow-free{display:none;}
  .hero h1{
    font-family:var(--display);
    font-size:clamp(28px, 3.4vw, 40px);
    line-height:1.12;
    margin:0 0 14px;
    font-weight:700;
    letter-spacing:-0.02em;
    text-wrap:balance;
  }
  .hero p{color:var(--muted); max-width:68ch; margin:0 0 6px; font-size:16.5px;}
  .hero p strong{color:var(--text);}
  .hero .source-note{font-size:13.5px; color:var(--muted); margin-top:18px; line-height:1.9;}

  .section-head{
    display:flex;
    align-items:baseline;
    gap:12px;
    margin:44px 0 14px;
    padding-bottom:12px;
    border-bottom:2px solid var(--text);
  }
  .section-head .num{font-family:var(--display); color:var(--accent); font-size:17px; font-weight:700; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;}
  .section-head h2{font-family:var(--display); font-size:26px; line-height:1.2; margin:0; font-weight:700; letter-spacing:-0.015em;}
  .section-head .count{margin-left:auto; font-size:13.5px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--muted); white-space:nowrap;}

  .qcard{
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:14px;
    background:var(--panel);
    margin-bottom:10px;
    overflow:hidden;
    box-shadow:var(--shadow);
  }
  .qcard:hover{border-color:var(--accent);}
  .qcard.open{border-color:var(--accent); box-shadow:inset 4px 0 0 var(--accent), var(--shadow);}
  .qcard.focused{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:1px;}
  .qhead{
    display:flex;
    align-items:flex-start;
    gap:14px;
    padding:15px 18px;
    cursor:pointer;
    user-select:none;
  }
  .qcheck{
    margin-top:3px;
    flex:0 0 auto;
    width:20px;height:20px;
    border-radius:6px;
    border:1.5px solid var(--muted);
    display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;
    cursor:pointer;
    background:var(--panel);
  }
  .qcheck:hover{border-color:var(--ok);}
  .qcheck.done{background:var(--ok); border-color:var(--ok);}
  .qcheck.done::after{content:"✓"; color:var(--panel); font-size:13px; font-weight:700;}
  .qmain{flex:1; min-width:0; display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:5px;}
  .qtext{flex:1; font-size:16.5px; line-height:1.4; font-weight:700;}
  .qtext.done-text{color:var(--muted); font-weight:500;}
  .qchips{display:flex; gap:6px; flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .qsec,.qcore{font-size:12px; padding:1px 8px; border-radius:99px; border:1px solid var(--border); color:var(--muted); background:var(--panel-2);}
  .qcore{color:var(--gold); border-color:var(--gold); background:var(--gold-soft);}
  .qsum{font-size:14.5px; color:var(--muted); line-height:1.5; max-width:var(--measure);}
  .qcard.open .qsum{display:none;}
  .qchevron{
    flex:0 0 auto;
    color:var(--muted);
    font-size:20px;
    line-height:1;
    transform:rotate(0deg);
    transition:transform .15s ease;
    margin-top:2px;
  }
  .qcard.open .qchevron{transform:rotate(90deg); color:var(--accent);}
  .qbody{
    display:none;
    padding:2px 22px 22px 52px;
    border-top:1px solid var(--border);
    font-size:16px;
    line-height:1.65;
  }
  .qcard.open .qbody{display:block; padding-top:18px;}
  /* Prose keeps a readable line length; tables, code and diagrams may use the full card width. */
  .qbody > p, .qbody > ul, .qbody > ol, .qbody > blockquote, .qbody > .callout, .qbody > h3, .qbody > h4{max-width:var(--measure);}
  .qbody p{margin:0 0 14px;}
  .qbody ul, .qbody ol{margin:0 0 14px; padding-left:22px;}
  .qbody li{margin-bottom:7px;}
  .qbody li::marker{color:var(--accent);}
  .qbody strong{color:var(--text); font-weight:700;}
  .qbody h3, .qbody h4{font-family:var(--display); font-size:17px; margin:20px 0 8px; letter-spacing:-0.01em;}
  code{
    font-family:var(--mono);
    background:var(--code-bg);
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    padding:0 5px;
    border-radius:5px;
    font-size:0.875em;
    overflow-wrap:anywhere;
  }
  pre{
    font-family:var(--mono);
    background:var(--code-bg);
    color:var(--text);
    padding:14px 16px;
    border-radius:10px;
    overflow-x:auto;
    font-size:13.5px;
    line-height:1.65;
    margin:0 0 16px;
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    tab-size:2;
  }
  pre code{background:none; border:0; padding:0; font-size:inherit;}
  /* syntax colouring added by the engine (comments, strings, keywords, numbers) */
  .tk-c{color:var(--muted); font-style:italic;}
  .tk-s{color:var(--ok);}
  .tk-k{color:var(--accent); font-weight:500;}
  .tk-n{color:var(--gold);}
  /* A diagram is a whiteboard (a chalkboard in dark mode): engine.js redraws the tidy SVG by hand
     (see "sketch" there) and this sets the board, the marker strokes and the handwriting. */
  .diagram{
    background:var(--panel);
    border:1.5px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:14px;
    box-shadow:inset 0 0 0 4px var(--panel), inset 0 0 0 5px var(--panel-2);
    padding:16px;
    margin:0 0 16px;
    overflow-x:auto;
  }
  .diagram svg{display:block; margin:0 auto; max-width:100%; height:auto;}
  /* Handwriting is sized by x-height (font-size-adjust) so it reads as large as the type it replaces.
     These values are the largest at which every label in every guide still fits its box:
     `node scripts/study/audit-diagrams.mjs` proves it, so re-run that after changing them. */
  .diagram svg.sk text:not(.sk-code){font-family:var(--hand); font-size-adjust:.50; font-weight:600; letter-spacing:.012em;}
  .diagram svg.sk text[font-family="var(--mono)"]:not(.sk-code){font-size-adjust:.60;}
  .diagram svg.sk text.sk-caps:not(.sk-code){font-size-adjust:.44;}
  .diagram svg.sk text[font-weight="600"]:not(.sk-code), .diagram svg.sk text[font-weight="700"]:not(.sk-code){font-weight:700;}
  /* Code and SQL are never handwritten (engine.js sketchIsCode): .sk-code keeps the authored type. */
  .diagram svg.sk .sk-s{stroke-width:1.9px; stroke-linecap:round; stroke-linejoin:round;}
  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference){
    .diagram svg.sk .sk-d{animation:sk-draw .5s ease-out backwards; animation-delay:var(--d, 0ms);}
    .diagram svg.sk .sk-t{animation:sk-ink .35s ease-out backwards; animation-delay:var(--d, 0ms);}
  }
  @keyframes sk-draw{ from{stroke-dasharray:1; stroke-dashoffset:1; fill-opacity:0;} to{stroke-dasharray:1; stroke-dashoffset:0;} }
  @keyframes sk-ink{ from{opacity:0;} }
  /* The tidy original stays one click away (the switch under each diagram), drawn exactly as authored. */
  .diagram.tidy{background:var(--panel-2); border-width:1px; border-radius:12px; box-shadow:none;}
  .dg-bar{display:flex; justify-content:flex-end; gap:4px; margin:10px 0 -4px; position:sticky; left:0;}
  .dg-bar button{
    font:500 11.5px/1 var(--sans); color:var(--muted); background:transparent; cursor:pointer;
    border:1px solid transparent; border-radius:999px; padding:5px 9px;
  }
  .dg-bar button:hover{color:var(--text); border-color:var(--border);}
  .dg-bar button[aria-pressed="true"]{color:var(--accent); background:var(--accent-soft); border-color:transparent;}
  .dg-bar button:focus-visible{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:1px;}
  .dg-bar button[data-dg="zoom"]{margin-left:6px; border-color:var(--border);}
  /* On a phone a 900-unit drawing squeezed into 300px is unreadable, so it keeps a readable size
     and scrolls sideways inside its board instead. */
  @media (max-width:760px){ .diagram svg{min-width:680px;} }
  /* Enlarged view (engine.js enlargeDiagram) */
  .dg-zoom{
    width:min(1500px, calc(100vw - 24px)); max-width:none; max-height:calc(100vh - 24px); padding:0;
    border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:16px; background:var(--bg); color:var(--text); overflow:hidden;
  }
  .dg-zoom[open]{display:flex; flex-direction:column;}
  .dg-zoom::backdrop{background:rgba(10,16,30,.6);}
  .dg-zoom-top{
    display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between; gap:12px; padding:8px 10px 8px 16px;
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--border); font:500 12.5px/1.3 var(--sans); color:var(--muted);
  }
  .dg-zoom-close{
    font:600 13px/1 var(--sans); color:var(--text); background:var(--panel); cursor:pointer;
    border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:999px; padding:9px 14px;
  }
  .dg-zoom-close:hover{border-color:var(--accent); color:var(--accent);}
  .dg-zoom-close:focus-visible, .dg-zoom-body:focus-visible{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:-2px;}
  .dg-zoom-body{overflow:auto; padding:14px;}
  .dg-zoom .diagram{margin:0;}
  .dg-zoom .diagram svg{width:100%; min-width:860px; max-width:none;}
  .dg-zoom .dg-bar [data-dg="zoom"]{display:none;}
  .diagram.lightbg{background:#F8FAFC; border-color:#CBD5E1;}
  .diagram.lightbg .codelabel{color:#334155;}
  .tag{
    display:inline-block;
    font-size:12px;
    color:var(--gold);
    background:var(--gold-soft);
    border:1px solid var(--gold);
    border-radius:6px;
    padding:1px 7px;
    margin-bottom:10px;
  }
  .tscroll{overflow-x:auto; margin:0 0 16px;}
  .tscroll > table.cmp{margin:0;}
  table.cmp{
    width:100%;
    border-collapse:collapse;
    margin:0 0 16px;
    font-size:14.5px;
    line-height:1.5;
  }
  table.cmp th, table.cmp td{
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    padding:9px 12px;
    text-align:left;
    vertical-align:top;
  }
  table.cmp th{background:var(--panel-2); font-size:13.5px; font-weight:700;}
  table.cmp tr:nth-child(odd) td{background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--panel-2) 45%, transparent);}

  .tbadge{display:inline-block; font-size:12px; font-weight:700; color:var(--gold); background:var(--gold-soft); border:1px solid var(--gold); border-radius:99px; padding:2px 10px; margin-bottom:10px;}
  .deeper{margin-top:16px; padding-top:12px; border-top:1px dashed var(--border); font-size:14.5px; line-height:1.9;}
  .deeper + .deeper{margin-top:2px; padding-top:0; border-top:0;}
  a.go{color:var(--accent); text-decoration:none; border-bottom:1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 35%, transparent);}
  a.go:hover{border-bottom-color:var(--accent);}

  .search{width:100%; box-sizing:border-box; margin:0 0 14px; padding:10px 12px; font:inherit; font-size:14.5px; color:var(--text); background:var(--bg); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:10px;}
  .search::placeholder{color:var(--muted);}
  .search:focus{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:1px;}
  .qcheck:focus-visible{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:2px;}
  mark{background:var(--gold-soft); color:var(--text); border-radius:3px; padding:0 2px;}
  .toolbar{display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; align-items:center; gap:10px 16px; margin:0 0 18px; font-size:14px; color:var(--muted);}
  .toolbar .tmeta{font-size:13.5px; margin-right:auto;}
  .toolbar .tgroup{display:flex; gap:10px; align-items:center; flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .toolbar button{font:inherit; font-size:13.5px; color:var(--text); background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:8px; padding:6px 12px; cursor:pointer;}
  .toolbar button:hover{border-color:var(--accent); color:var(--accent);}
  .toolbar label{display:flex; gap:6px; align-items:center; cursor:pointer; white-space:nowrap;}
  .toolbar input{accent-color:var(--accent); width:15px; height:15px;}
  .empty{color:var(--muted); font-size:15px; padding:18px; border:1px dashed var(--border); border-radius:12px;}
  .pager{display:flex; justify-content:space-between; gap:12px; margin-top:28px;}
  .pager button{font:inherit; font-size:14.5px; font-weight:500; color:var(--accent); background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:10px; padding:12px 16px; cursor:pointer; max-width:48%; text-align:left;}
  .pager button:last-child{text-align:right;}
  .pager button:hover{border-color:var(--accent); background:var(--accent-soft);}
  .back-btn{position:fixed; right:22px; bottom:22px; z-index:10; font:inherit; font-size:14px; font-weight:700; color:var(--accent-ink); background:var(--accent); border:0; border-radius:99px; padding:11px 18px; cursor:pointer; box-shadow:0 6px 18px rgba(0,0,0,.22);}
  .keys{display:inline-block; margin-top:6px;}
  kbd{font-family:var(--mono); font-size:11.5px; padding:0 5px; border:1px solid var(--border); border-bottom-width:2px; border-radius:5px; background:var(--panel); color:var(--text);}
  .hero-actions{margin-top:18px; display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:10px;}
  .fc-start,.toolbar .flash-btn{font:inherit; font-weight:700; color:var(--accent-ink); background:var(--accent); border:1px solid var(--accent); border-radius:10px; cursor:pointer;}
  .fc-start{font-size:15px; padding:10px 18px;}
  .toolbar .flash-btn{color:var(--accent-ink);}
  .toolbar .flash-btn:hover{color:var(--accent-ink);}
  .fc-start:hover,.toolbar .flash-btn:hover{filter:brightness(1.1);}
  button.fc-start.alt{background:var(--panel); color:var(--accent); border:1px solid var(--accent);}
  button.fc-start.alt:hover{background:var(--accent-soft); filter:none;}
  a.fc-start.alt{display:inline-block; text-decoration:none; background:var(--panel); color:var(--accent); border:1px solid var(--accent);}

  /* ---------- Flashcards ---------- */
  body.fc-lock{overflow:hidden;}
  .fc{position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:50; background:rgba(8,14,26,.6); display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center; padding:24px;}
  .fc[hidden]{display:none;}
  .fc-dialog{width:min(920px,100%); max-height:100%; display:flex; flex-direction:column; background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:18px; box-shadow:0 24px 70px rgba(0,0,0,.4); outline:none;}
  .fc-head{display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:flex-start; gap:12px; padding:18px 22px 12px;}

      a:`<p>Class components had three named phases; function components get the same behavior out of <code>useEffect</code>'s dependency array.</p>
      <table class="cmp">
        <tr><th>Class lifecycle</th><th>Function component equivalent</th></tr>
        <tr><td><code>componentDidMount</code></td><td><code>useEffect(fn, [])</code> — empty array, runs once after first render</td></tr>

      </table>
      <p>One nuance worth probing for: leaving the dependency array off entirely makes the effect run after <em>every</em> render, which is different from both <code>[]</code> and a populated array — a common source of bugs.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>

        <li><strong>What causes an effect to run repeatedly?</strong> Most often a dependency that gets a new reference every render — an inline object, array, or function — so React sees it as "changed" even though its contents are the same.         <li><strong>How do you avoid race conditions in an effect?</strong> Use an <code>AbortController</code> (or a simple "is this still current" flag) created fresh each run and cleaned up in the effect's cleanup, so a stale response from a superseded request can't overwrite newer state.</li>
        <li><strong>When should you avoid useEffect?</strong> For anything computable directly during render (derived/filtered values) — that doesn't need to "synchronize with an external system" at all — and for event-specific logic, which belongs in the handler, not in an effect reacting to the state it caused.</li>

      q:"What is useRef used for beyond DOM references?",
      a:`<p>useRef stores any mutable value that persists across renders WITHOUT triggering re-renders. It's essentially an instance variable for function components.</p>
<pre>// 1. DOM reference (most common)
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

  isMounted.current = true;
  return () => { isMounted.current = false; };

      q:"When is useReducer a better fit than useState?",
      a:`<p>Reach for <code>useReducer</code> when state has multiple sub-values that change together, when the next state depends on complex logic around the previous state, or when you want the transitions themselves to be testable as a pure function separate from the component.</p>
<pre>type State = { status: "idle"|"loading"|"success"|"error"; data: unknown; error: string|null };
type Action =
  | { type: "FETCH_START" }
  | { type: "FETCH_SUCCESS"; payload: unknown }
  | { type: "FETCH_ERROR"; error: string };

function reducer(state: State, action: Action): State {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "FETCH_START": return { ...state, status: "loading", error: null };
    case "FETCH_SUCCESS": return { status: "success", data: action.payload, error: null };
    case "FETCH_ERROR": return { status: "error", data: null, error: action.error };
  }
}

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { status: "idle", data: null, error: null });</pre>
<p>It isn't "Redux in a component" — there's no store or middleware — but it borrows the same idea: a single pure function owns every valid transition, which makes impossible states (like <code>status: "success"</code> with no data) much harder to end up in by accident.</p>
<p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
<ul><li><strong>Can you combine it with Context?</strong> Yes — <code>useReducer</code> + Context is a common lightweight alternative to Redux for state shared across a subtree, without pulling in a library.</li></ul>`

      q:"How do you write a custom hook with solid TypeScript typing?",
      a:`<p>A custom hook is just a function that calls other hooks — the discipline is in the return type. For a public hook, type the return explicitly rather than leaning on inference, and use <code>as const</code> when returning a tuple so consumers get positional types instead of a wide array type.</p>
<pre>function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initialValue: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
    try {
      const item = window.localStorage.getItem(key);
      return item ? (JSON.parse(item) as T) : initialValue;
    } catch {
      return initialValue;
    }
  });

  const setAndPersist = useCallback((next: T | ((prev: T) => T)) => {
    setValue(prev => {
      const resolved = next instanceof Function ? next(prev) : next;
      window.localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(resolved));
      return resolved;
    });
  }, [key]);

  return [value, setAndPersist] as const; // a tuple, not (T | setter)[]
}</pre>
<ul>
<li>Return a <strong>tuple</strong> (<code>as const</code>) for two values with a clear order (mirrors <code>useState</code>); return an <strong>object</strong> once you have three or more, so call sites don't have to remember positional order.</li>
<li>Any hook touching <code>window</code>/<code>document</code> needs a guard or lazy initializer for environments (SSR) where those globals don't exist during the server render.</li>
<li><code>useRef</code> is the other building block custom hooks lean on — it holds a value (a previous value, an interval id, a "did this already run" flag) across renders <em>without</em> triggering a re-render when it changes, unlike state.</li>

      <pre>function reducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'increment': return state + 1;
    case 'double':    return state * 2;
    default:          return state; // no 'reset' case — falls through here
  }
}</pre>

      <p>The final value is <strong>3</strong>. The trap is assuming a <code>'reset'</code> action does something just because it sounds like it should — a reducer only does exactly what its <code>switch</code> handles, and anything else silently falls through to <code>default</code>.</p>

      a:`<div class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 560 200" width="560">

<p>RTK also ships <strong>RTK Query</strong> for server state, with the same caching/dedup/invalidation model as TanStack Query — worth mentioning that even inside a Redux-based app, server data still belongs in a query cache, not hand-rolled into slices.</p>`

      <p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> keeping selectors small and stable, and being careful about returning newly-created objects from a selector (breaks the equality check Zustand uses to decide whether to re-render).</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do you choose between Redux Toolkit, TanStack Query, Zustand, and Context for a given piece of state?",
      a:`<p>The senior framing: these solve different problems, and the most common mistake is using one tool for all of them — especially putting server data in Redux.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>TanStack/React Query:</strong> the default for <em>server</em> state — anything that's a cached copy of data owned by an API. Gives you stale-while-revalidate caching, retries, dedup, pagination, and optimistic updates for free.</li>
<li><strong>Redux Toolkit:</strong> global <em>client</em> state with non-trivial derived data and a need for strict, traceable, unidirectional flow — a shopping cart, a multi-step wizard, feature flags. Heavier setup, but strong devtools and conventions at scale.</li>
<li><strong>Zustand:</strong> lightweight global client state with near-zero boilerplate and no Provider — a good default for things like theme, sidebar/modal state, or small shared state that doesn't need Redux's ceremony.</li>
<li><strong>Context:</strong> best thought of as dependency injection, not a state manager — it re-renders every consumer when its value changes, regardless of which part they read. Fine for values that change rarely (theme, locale, the authenticated user).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Golden rule:</strong> server state ≠ client state. If it came from an API, it belongs in a query cache (React Query/SWR), not in Redux.</p>`

      q:"What is the difference between local and global state management?",

      <p>Global client state is shared across distant parts of the application, like authenticated-user context or a multi-page workflow. I'd reach for something like Zustand or Redux only when that shared state is complex enough to justify it. Server data should be treated as server state, with a tool like React Query, rather than copied unnecessarily into a global client store.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is prop drilling?",
      a:`<p>Prop drilling is when data or callbacks have to pass through several intermediate components just so a deeply nested component can use them — the components in between don't need the value themselves, they just keep forwarding it.</p>
      <p>For a short, clear component chain, passing props is fine. If the value is genuinely cross-cutting or widely shared, component composition, React Context, or a state-management store usually gives a cleaner design.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do you pass data from a child component to its parent in React?",
      a:`<p>React uses one-way data flow, so the parent passes a callback down to the child as a prop. The child calls that callback with the new value or event data, and the parent updates its own state.</p>
      <p>If the components are unrelated or far apart in the tree, I'd consider lifting the state to the closest common ancestor, or using Context or an appropriate shared store instead of threading a callback through several layers.</p>`
    },

      q:"How do you pass data between sibling components, like a Search box and a ProductList?",

<ol>

No new infrastructure, and it's exactly what "lift state up" means in the React docs.</li>
<li><strong>React Context.</strong> Same idea, but skips prop drilling once the common ancestor is several levels away from one or both components — reach for it once drilling actually hurts, not preemptively.</li>
<li><strong>URL / query params.</strong> Both components read/write the same URL (<code>?q=lipstick</code>) via <code>useSearchParams</code>. The search becomes bookmarkable and survives a refresh, which local state never does.</li>
<li><strong>A global store</strong> (Zustand/Redux). Only justified once <code>searchValue</code> needs to be read or written from unrelated parts of the app, not just these two components.</li>

<pre><code>function App() {
  const [searchValue, setSearchValue] = useState("");
  return (
    <>
      <Search value={searchValue} onChange={setSearchValue} />

<p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Why not just fetch on every keystroke?</strong> Keep the input's own value updating immediately (an "onChange" state), but only trigger the actual search/fetch on an explicit submit (button click or Enter) unless live-as-you-type search is a real requirement — otherwise debounce it (see the JavaScript track's debounce question).</li>
<li><strong>How would you implement the fetch itself?</strong> A <code>try/catch/finally</code> around <code>fetch</code>, checking <code>response.ok</code>, setting loading/error/data state — see the "Fetch data and render it in a table" question in the Coding Exercise track for the full pattern, including cancellation with <code>AbortController</code>.</li>

    },
    {
      q:"How do you handle asynchronous calls and their state in Redux?",
      a:`<p>Reducers must stay synchronous and free of side effects — they can't call <code>fetch</code> themselves. <pre><code>// Redux Toolkit's createAsyncThunk generates pending/fulfilled/rejected
// action types automatically from one async function.
const fetchProducts = createAsyncThunk("products/fetch", async (query) => {
  const res = await fetch("/api/products?q=" + encodeURIComponent(query));
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);
  return res.json();
});

  name: "products",
  initialState: { items: [], status: "idle", error: null },
  reducers: {},
  extraReducers: (builder) => {
    builder
      .addCase(fetchProducts.pending, (state) => {
        state.status = "loading";
        state.error = null;
      })
      .addCase(fetchProducts.fulfilled, (state, action) => {
        state.status = "succeeded";
        state.items = action.payload;
      })
      .addCase(fetchProducts.rejected, (state, action) => {
        state.status = "failed";
        state.error = action.error.message;
      });
  },

<ul>
<li><strong>Thunk vs. Saga?</strong> A thunk is a plain async function — perfectly fine for straightforward request/response logic. Saga uses generator-based effects for more complex orchestration (debouncing, cancellation, coordinating multiple sagas) — more power, more ceremony. Most teams default to thunks and only reach for Saga once that orchestration complexity is real.</li>
<li><strong>How do you avoid a stale response overwriting a newer one?</strong> Redux Toolkit's <code>createAsyncThunk</code> accepts an <code>AbortSignal</code> via <code>thunkAPI.signal</code> — cancel the previous request the same way you would with a plain <code>AbortController</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Isn't this what RTK Query is for?</strong> Yes — RTK Query generates this exact pending/fulfilled/rejected lifecycle (plus caching, refetching, and cache invalidation) from just an endpoint definition, so most new Redux code doesn't hand-write thunks for data-fetching anymore.</li>
</ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"Why is Context API bad for frequently changing state?",
      a:`<p>Context re-renders ALL consumers whenever the provider value changes, even if a consumer only uses a small part of the state.</p>
<pre>// ❌ BAD: All consumers re-render when ANY part of this changes
const AppContext = createContext({ user: null, theme: 'dark', count: 0 });

// ✅ SOLUTION 1: Split into separate contexts
const UserContext = createContext(null);
const ThemeContext = createContext('dark');

// ✅ SOLUTION 2: Use useMemo on the provider value
function AppProvider({ children }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user]);
  return <UserContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</UserContext.Provider>;
}

// ✅ SOLUTION 3: Use Zustand instead (no provider, no re-render issue)
const useStore = create((set) => ({
  count: 0,
  increment: () => set((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 })),
}));</pre>
<p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> This is a trap question. Many devs use Context for everything. Show you know its re-rendering limitation and when to reach for Zustand or jotai instead.</p>`
    }
  ]
},

    {
      q:"How would you show whichever of two independent API results arrives first, then append the second — without one failure blocking the other?",
      a:`<p>Start both requests concurrently and update state from each one's own completion handler, instead of waiting for an aggregate like <code>Promise.all</code> (which waits for both, and rejects the whole batch if either one fails). Functional state updates let each source append independently without clobbering the other's result, and an <code>AbortController</code> plus an "is this still the active search" check protects against a stale, slower request overwriting a newer one.</p>
<pre><code>function useProgressiveSearch() {
  const [products, setProducts] = useState([]);
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState([]);
  const [pending, setPending] = useState(0);
  const activeRequest = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => () => activeRequest.current?.abort(), []);

  function search(query) {
    activeRequest.current?.abort();
    const controller = new AbortController();
    activeRequest.current = controller;

    setProducts([]);
    setErrors([]);
    setPending(2);

    const isCurrent = () => activeRequest.current === controller;

    async function loadSource(source) {
      try {
        const url = "/api/products/" + source + "?q=" + encodeURIComponent(query);
        const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status);
        const items = await res.json();
        if (isCurrent()) setProducts((prev) => [...prev, ...items.map((item) => ({ ...item, source }))]);
      } catch (err) {
        if (isCurrent()) setErrors((prev) => [...prev, err.message]);
      } finally {
        if (isCurrent()) setPending((count) => count - 1);
      }
    }

    loadSource("source-a");
    loadSource("source-b");
  }

  return { products, errors, loading: pending > 0, search };
}</code></pre>
<p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Why not just use <code>Promise.all</code>?</strong> It waits for the slowest of the two before rendering anything, and a single rejection fails the whole batch — the opposite of "show whichever arrives first."</li>
<li><strong>What does <code>Promise.allSettled</code> give you instead?</strong> The final outcome of every promise regardless of failures, but still only after ALL of them settle — it doesn't give progressive, as-they-arrive rendering either.</li>
<li><strong>How do you avoid duplicate ids across the two sources?</strong> Tag each item with its source when appending (<code>{ ...item, source }</code>) and key rendered rows by <code>source + ":" + id</code> rather than assuming ids are globally unique.</li>
</ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do pagination, sorting and filters work on a search results page backed by GraphQL?",
      a:`<p>The design principle: the <strong>server owns the result set, the facets and the pagination state</strong>; the client sends the current criteria and renders what comes back, so the grid and the available facets update together.</p>
<pre>query Search($q: String!, $filters: [FilterInput!], $sort: SortOption, $page: Int, $pageSize: Int) {
  search(query: $q, filters: $filters, sort: $sort, page: $page, pageSize: $pageSize) {
    items { id ...ProductCard }
    facets { name values { value label count selected } }
    pageInfo { page pageSize totalPages totalItems }
  }
}</pre>
<ul>
<li><strong>Reset to page 1</strong> when the query, filters or sort change, otherwise a user on page 5 filters down to two pages and sees an empty result. Use the returned <code>pageInfo</code> (and clamp) rather than guessing the page count.</li>
<li><strong>Facet counts come from the server</strong> and reflect the other active filters.</li>
<li><strong>Offset vs cursor:</strong> page numbers suit shopping search where users jump to a page and want a total; cursor pagination is stable when data changes and cheaper for deep or infinite lists but cannot jump to page N.</li>
<li><strong>Race conditions:</strong> a slow older response must not overwrite a newer one. Cancel with <code>AbortController</code> or ignore superseded requests; client libraries keyed by variables handle this.</li>
<li><strong>Keep previous results on screen while loading</strong> (<code>keepPreviousData</code> or <code>useTransition</code>) to avoid the grid flashing empty.</li>
<li><strong>Sort on the server.</strong> Sorting only the current page client-side is wrong. Debounce text input, apply checkboxes immediately.</li>
<li><strong>Accessibility:</strong> announce "24 results" in an <code>aria-live="polite"</code> region, keep focus stable after re-render, use fieldset/legend or disclosure buttons for facet groups.</li>
<li><strong>SEO:</strong> paginated URLs should be crawlable with canonical tags; decide which facet combinations are indexable.</li>
</ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"Show React Query with optimistic updates + rollback.",
      a:`<p>Optimistic updates make the UI feel instant by updating the cache before the server responds, with rollback on failure.</p>
<pre>const qc = useQueryClient();

const { mutate } = useMutation({
  mutationFn: updateTodo,
  onMutate: async (newTodo) => {
    // 1. Cancel in-flight refetches so they don't overwrite our optimistic update
    await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['todos', newTodo.id] });

    // 2. Snapshot the previous value for rollback
    const previousTodo = qc.getQueryData(['todos', newTodo.id]);

    // 3. Optimistically update the cache
    qc.setQueryData(['todos', newTodo.id], (old: Todo) => ({
      ...old,
      ...newTodo,
    }));

    return { previousTodo }; // context for onError
  },
  onError: (_err, newTodo, context) => {
    // 4. Rollback on error
    qc.setQueryData(['todos', newTodo.id], context?.previousTodo);
    toast.error('Update failed, reverted changes');
  },
  onSettled: (_data, _err, newTodo) => {
    // 5. Always refetch to ensure server/client sync
    qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos', newTodo.id] });
  },
});</pre>
<p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> This is a very common senior interview question. Remember the 5 steps: cancel, snapshot, optimistic update, rollback on error, refetch on settle.</p>`
    },

      a:`<p>Production-grade API calls need request cancellation, retry logic for transient failures, and runtime type validation.</p>
<pre>import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.number(),
  name: z.string(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  role: z.enum(['admin', 'user', 'viewer']),
});

type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>; // auto-generate TypeScript type

async function getUser(id: number, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<User> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(\`/api/users/\${id}\`, { signal });

    if (res.ok) {
      const data = await res.json();
      return UserSchema.parse(data); // runtime validation!
    }

    if (res.status >= 400 && res.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(\`Client error: \${res.status}\`); // don't retry 4xx
    }

    // Exponential backoff for 5xx
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1000 * Math.pow(2, attempt)));
  }
  throw new Error('Retries exhausted');
}

// Usage with AbortController (cleanup on unmount)
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  getUser(1, controller.signal).then(setUser).catch(console.error);
  return () => controller.abort(); // cancel if component unmounts
}, []);</pre>
<p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> Three things interviewers look for: (1) AbortController for cleanup, (2) only retry server errors, (3) runtime validation with Zod to bridge the TS/runtime gap.</p>`

      q:"What are React Server Components, and how do they differ from traditional SSR?",
      a:`<p>Traditional SSR renders the whole tree to HTML on the server for the initial load, then ships the same component code to the client for hydration. React Server Components (RSC) let specific components run <em>only</em> on the server — including direct data access — and never ship their code to the client at all, composed in the same tree alongside regular Client Components that do hydrate.</p>
      <p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> "RSC reduces client bundle size since server-only code never reaches the browser" and "it's a per-component choice, not a whole-page one" — this is what Next.js's App Router builds on.</p>
      <table class="cmp">
<tr><th>Strategy</th><th>When HTML is generated</th><th>Best for</th></tr>
<tr><td>SSR</td><td>On every request</td><td>Personalized/auth-gated pages, dashboards</td></tr>
<tr><td>SSG</td><td>At build time</td><td>Marketing pages, docs, blogs</td></tr>
<tr><td>ISR</td><td>Build time, then revalidated on a timer (e.g. every 60s)</td><td>Semi-static data like product pages</td></tr>
<tr><td>Server Components</td><td>Per-request, per-component — a finer grain than "the page"</td><td>Anything that doesn't need client interactivity or state</td></tr>
</table>
<p>In the Next.js App Router, every component is a Server Component by default; a leaf component opts into the client with <code>"use client"</code> only when it needs state, effects, or browser APIs — Server Components can import Client Components, but never the other way around.</p>
<pre>// Server Component (default) — can query a database directly
async function ProductPage({ params }) {
  const product = await db.query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = $1", [params.id]);
  return (<div><h1>{product.name}</h1><AddToCartButton productId={product.id} /></div>);
}

// "use server" — a Server Action callable directly from a Client Component
"use server";
async function addToCart(productId) {
  await db.insert("cart_items", { productId, userId: getCurrentUser() });
  revalidatePath("/cart");
}</pre>
<p>This also enables <strong>streaming SSR</strong>: the server sends the page shell immediately and streams in each <code>Suspense</code> boundary's content as it resolves (Next.js's <code>loading.tsx</code> wires this in automatically), instead of blocking the entire response on the slowest data fetch.</p>`

    {
      q:"What are useTransition and useDeferredValue, and when would you reach for them?",
      a:`<p>Both are React 18+ concurrent-rendering APIs for keeping the UI responsive when a state update triggers expensive work. They don't make anything faster — they let React deprioritize the expensive part so urgent updates (typing, clicks) still render immediately.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>useTransition:</strong> marks a state update as non-urgent. React renders it in the background and can interrupt it if a more urgent update comes in, while an <code>isPending</code> flag lets you show a loading indicator.</li>
<li><strong>useDeferredValue:</strong> takes a value you don't control the setter for (e.g. a prop) and returns a version that "lags behind" during heavy renders, so whatever drives that value stays responsive.</li>
</ul>
<pre>const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

function handleChange(e) {
  setQuery(e.target.value);            // urgent: input stays responsive
  startTransition(() => {
    setFilteredResults(filterHugeList(e.target.value)); // non-urgent
  });
}</pre>
<p>Rule of thumb: <code>useTransition</code> when you control the state update; <code>useDeferredValue</code> when you only have the value (e.g. it's a prop or comes from a store).</p>
<p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
<ul><li><strong>Does this replace debouncing?</strong> No — debouncing delays work, transitions deprioritize it while still using the latest value. They solve different problems and are often combined.</li></ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is React Fiber, and how does it enable concurrent rendering?",
      a:`<p>Fiber is React's reconciliation engine (since React 16) — it replaced the older "stack reconciler," which rendered synchronously and recursively, so a large component tree could block the main thread and drop frames.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Units of work:</strong> Fiber breaks rendering into small units, roughly one per component, each a node in a linked-list-like structure. React can pause after any unit and hand control back to the browser.</li>
<li><strong>Interruptible rendering:</strong> because the work is chunked, React can pause a low-priority render to handle an urgent update (a keystroke) and resume — or discard in-progress work entirely if it's no longer needed.</li>
<li><strong>Time slicing:</strong> React yields to the browser every few milliseconds during a render pass, so animations and input stay smooth even under a heavy update.</li>
</ul>
<p>Fiber is the underlying mechanism that makes <code>useTransition</code>, <code>useDeferredValue</code>, and Suspense possible — none of them would work with the old synchronous renderer, since there'd be nothing to interrupt.</p>`

    {

  addOptimistic({ id: Date.now(), text, isPending: true }); // 1. instant UI update
  await saveComment(text);                                  // 2. reconciles or rolls back automatically

      <p>It takes the current confirmed state plus an update function, and returns a temporary "optimistic" state that reflects your update right away. If the underlying async action succeeds, the real state (passed in as the first argument) eventually catches up and replaces the optimistic value. If it fails, React discards the optimistic update and the UI reverts to the last confirmed state — no manual rollback code required.</p>

      <pre>const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(signUpAction, initialState);

  const { pending } = useFormStatus(); // no props needed
  return <button disabled={pending}>Submit</button>;

function Message({ promise }) {
  const data = use(promise); // suspends until resolved
  return <div>{data}</div>;

      <ul>
        <li><strong>How does <code>use()</code> differ from <code>await</code>?</strong> Both unwrap a Promise, but <code>use()</code> works inside ordinary Client Components by suspending the render tree, while <code>await</code> in a component body only works in async Server Components.</li>
        <li><strong>Can you call <code>use()</code> conditionally?</strong> Yes — unlike other hooks, <code>use()</code> can be called inside loops and <code>if</code> blocks, since it isn't bound by the Rules of Hooks the way <code>useState</code>/<code>useEffect</code> are.</li>

    {
      q:"Why use useDeferredValue instead of debouncing a search input?",
      a:`<p>They solve different problems. <strong>Debounce</strong> delays <em>when work starts</em> by a fixed time, so every keystroke waits (for example 300 ms) even on a fast device. <strong><code>useDeferredValue</code></strong> lets the input update immediately at urgent priority, while the expensive render that depends on the value happens at lower priority and can be interrupted.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>No artificial delay:</strong> on a fast machine the deferred render finishes quickly; on a slow one it lags behind without blocking typing. A debounce timer is the same fixed wait for everyone.</li>
<li><strong>Interruptible:</strong> if the user types again mid-render, React abandons the stale render and starts over. A debounced handler that already started heavy work cannot be cancelled.</li>
<li><strong>It does not reduce network requests.</strong> It defers <em>rendering</em>. If each keystroke triggers a fetch, you still want a debounce or an aborted request, and can combine both.</li>
<li><strong>Use it</strong> for a child that receives a query prop, a large filtered list you own, or expensive tab content. For third-party state you cannot wrap, or things that must not run at all until the user pauses (API calls), debounce is the right tool.</li>
</ul>
<pre>function Search({ items }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);              // lags behind during heavy renders
  const results = useMemo(() => filter(items, deferred), [items, deferred]);
  const stale = query !== deferred;
  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} />
      <div style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.6 : 1 }}><List results={results} /></div>
    </>
  );
}</pre>`

      q:"What is the Compound Component pattern, and when is it worth reaching for?",
      a:`<p>Compound components share implicit state through Context between a parent and a set of children, so consumers can compose the pieces freely instead of passing one big config object through a single prop.</p>
<pre>const AccordionCtx = createContext(null);

function Accordion({ children }) {
  const [openId, setOpenId] = useState(null);
  const toggle = id => setOpenId(prev => (prev === id ? null : id));
  return <AccordionCtx.Provider value={{ openId, toggle }}>{children}</AccordionCtx.Provider>;
}

function AccordionItem({ id, title, children }) {
  const { openId, toggle } = useContext(AccordionCtx);
  const isOpen = openId === id;
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => toggle(id)}>{title}</button>
      {isOpen && <div>{children}</div>}
    </div>
  );
}

// <Accordion><AccordionItem id="1" title="Section 1">...</AccordionItem></Accordion></pre>
<p>It's the pattern behind most headless UI libraries (Radix, Reach UI, Headless UI) — it gives consumers control over markup and layout while the parent still owns the shared state. const app = () => <div>Hi</div>;
<app />  // compiles to React.createElement('app', ...)
         // React looks for an HTML tag called "app" — doesn't exist, breaks

// Capitalized — compiles to a component reference
const App = () => <div>Hi</div>;
<App />  // compiles to React.createElement(App, ...)
         // React calls your function as intended</pre>
      <p>A lowercase tag like <code><app /></code> is compiled as a string — the name of an HTML element — not a reference to your variable. Since there's no built-in <code><app></code> element, this silently fails to render your component instead of throwing a helpful error.</p>

<pre>import { forwardRef, useRef } from 'react';

// Pattern: assertion to recover generics
type ListProps<T> = { items: T[]; renderItem: (item: T) => React.ReactNode };

function ListInner<T>(props: ListProps<T> & { ref?: React.Ref<HTMLUListElement> }) {
  return (
    <ul ref={props.ref}>

// For React 18, use the module augmentation or casting pattern.</pre>

<pre>// Render Props pattern
function MouseTracker({ render }: {
  render: (pos: { x: number; y: number }) => React.ReactNode
}) {
  const [pos, setPos] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  useEffect(() => {
    const handler = (e: MouseEvent) => setPos({ x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY });
    window.addEventListener('mousemove', handler);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('mousemove', handler);
  }, []);
  return <>{render(pos)}</>;
}

// Usage
<MouseTracker render={({ x, y }) => <p>Mouse: {x}, {y}</p>} />

// ✅ Modern equivalent: custom hook (preferred)
function useMousePosition() {
  const [pos, setPos] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  useEffect(() => { /* same listener logic */ }, []);
  return pos;
}
const { x, y } = useMousePosition();</pre>

          {options.map((opt, i) => (
            <li key={opt} role="option" aria-selected={opt === value}>{opt}</li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </>
  );
}</pre>
<p>The essentials: <code>role="combobox"</code> on the trigger with <code>aria-expanded</code>/<code>aria-controls</code>, <code>role="listbox"</code>/<code>role="option"</code> with <code>aria-selected</code> on the list, and arrow-key/Enter/Escape handling. In real projects, reach for Radix UI or Headless UI instead of hand-rolling this — but the ARIA pattern is what the question is actually testing.</p>`

      q:"What security headers should every React app have?",
      a:`<p>Security headers are your first line of defense. Configure them in your web server or Next.js middleware.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Content-Security-Policy (CSP):</strong> Whitelist allowed script/style sources. Prevents inline script injection.</li>
<li><strong>X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff:</strong> Prevents MIME type sniffing attacks.</li>
<li><strong>X-Frame-Options: DENY:</strong> Prevents clickjacking by blocking iframe embedding.</li>
<li><strong>Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS):</strong> Forces HTTPS for all future requests.</li>
<li><strong>Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin:</strong> Controls what referrer info is sent.</li>
<li><strong>Permissions-Policy:</strong> Disable unused browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation).</li>
</ul>`

      q:"How can you still get XSS in a React app?",
      a:`<p class="lede">React escapes values rendered as text, which blocks the classic case. The remaining holes are places where you hand it raw HTML, URLs or scripts.</p><table class="cmp"><tr><th>Hole</th><th>Example</th><th>Fix</th></tr><tr><td><code>dangerouslySetInnerHTML</code></td><td>rendering user or CMS HTML</td><td>sanitize with DOMPurify (allowlist tags), or render Markdown safely</td></tr><tr><td>URL attributes</td><td><code><a href={userUrl}></code> with <code>javascript:...</code></td><td>validate the protocol (allow http, https, mailto) before rendering</td></tr><tr><td>Serialized state in HTML</td><td><code>window.__STATE__ = \${JSON.stringify(data)}</code> can contain <code></script></code></td><td>escape <code><</code> (use serialize-javascript) or pass data through a JSON script tag</td></tr><tr><td>Direct DOM / third parties</td><td><code>ref.current.innerHTML = ...</code>, unvetted script tags, compromised packages</td><td>avoid innerHTML, use CSP and Subresource Integrity, audit dependencies</td></tr><tr><td><code>eval</code> and <code>new Function</code></td><td>building code from strings</td><td>never; use data and lookups</td></tr></table><ul><li>Add a <strong>Content Security Policy</strong> as a second layer, and store session tokens in <code>HttpOnly</code> cookies so an XSS bug cannot read them.</li><li>Server Components and Server Actions do not remove the need to validate and encode; the boundary still receives untrusted data.</li></ul><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> "React escapes text by default; I audit every dangerouslySetInnerHTML, every user-controlled URL, and how server data is embedded in the HTML."</p>`

      q:"When should you use ARIA, and what are its rules?",
      a:`<ul><li><strong>First rule of ARIA:</strong> do not use it if a native element works. A <code><button></code> already has the role, keyboard support and focus; <code><div role="button"></code> needs all of that rebuilt by hand.</li><li><strong>Roles</strong> say what something is (<code>dialog</code>, <code>tablist</code>), <strong>states</strong> say how it is now (<code>aria-expanded</code>, <code>aria-selected</code>, <code>aria-invalid</code>), <strong>properties</strong> relate things (<code>aria-labelledby</code>, <code>aria-describedby</code>, <code>aria-controls</code>).</li><li><strong>ARIA changes only what assistive tech hears</strong>, not behaviour: you still implement keyboard handling (Arrow keys, Escape, Tab order) and focus management.</li><li><strong>Live regions</strong> (<code>aria-live="polite"</code>, <code>role="status"</code>) announce updates such as form errors and toasts.</li><li>Visible labels beat <code>aria-label</code>; hide decoration with <code>aria-hidden="true"</code> (never on focusable elements).</li></ul><pre><button aria-expanded={open} aria-controls="menu" onClick={() => setOpen(!open)}>Menu</button>
<ul id="menu" hidden={!open}>…</ul>

<p role="status" aria-live="polite">{saved ? 'Saved' : ''}</p></pre><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> Test with the keyboard only, then a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver) and an automated pass (axe); automation catches roughly a third of problems, not all.</p>`

  id:"test-rtl", title:"React Testing Library",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"How do you test a component that fetches data asynchronously with React Testing Library?",
      a:`<p>Use <code>findBy*</code> queries, which retry until an element appears (up to a timeout), for anything that only exists after an async update. Mock the network at the network layer with MSW (Mock Service Worker) rather than mocking <code>fetch</code> directly — MSW intercepts real requests, so the component's actual fetch code runs unmodified.</p>
<pre>const server = setupServer(
  http.get("/api/user/1", () => HttpResponse.json({ name: "Dana", role: "admin" }))
);
beforeAll(() => server.listen());
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test("shows user data after loading", async () => {
  render(<UserProfile userId="1" />);
  expect(screen.getByRole("status")).toBeInTheDocument(); // loading state first

  expect(await screen.findByText(/dana/i)).toBeInTheDocument(); // waits for it
  expect(screen.queryByRole("status")).not.toBeInTheDocument(); // loading is gone
});

test("shows an error on failure", async () => {
  server.use(http.get("/api/user/1", () => HttpResponse.error()));
  render(<UserProfile userId="1" />);
  expect(await screen.findByText(/something went wrong/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});</pre>
<p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
<ul><li><strong>Why not just mock fetch with jest.mock?</strong> It couples the test to implementation details (exactly how the component calls fetch) instead of behavior, and doesn't catch request-shape bugs (wrong URL, missing header) the way a real intercepted request does.</li></ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"RTL query priority — which query should you reach for first, and why?",
      a:`<p>RTL's queries aren't interchangeable — they exist in a deliberate priority order that mirrors how real users and assistive technology perceive the page.</p>
      <table class="cmp">
        <tr><th>Priority</th><th>Query</th><th>Use when</th></tr>
        <tr><td>1</td><td><code>getByRole</code></td><td>Almost always — mirrors how screen readers traverse the DOM by ARIA role</td></tr>
        <tr><td>2</td><td><code>getByLabelText</code></td><td>Form inputs tied to a <code><label></code> — also enforces that the label/input association actually exists</td></tr>
        <tr><td>3</td><td><code>getByText</code></td><td>Non-interactive visible text — paragraphs, headings, static copy</td></tr>
        <tr><td>4</td><td><code>getByTestId</code></td><td>Last resort — nothing else uniquely identifies the element; not visible to real users</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p>Every <code>getBy*</code> also has a <code>findBy*</code> (async, waits for the element) and a <code>queryBy*</code> (returns <code>null</code> instead of throwing) variant, so the priority order applies regardless of which timing variant you need.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Why is <code>getByTestId</code> ranked last, not banned?</strong> It couples the test to implementation rather than to what a user can see, so refactors that don't change behavior can still break the test. It's fine as an escape hatch when no accessible query can uniquely identify the element.</li>
        <li><strong>Why does <code>getByLabelText</code> outrank <code>getByText</code>?</strong> Because it verifies real accessibility wiring — if the label isn't correctly associated with the input, the query fails, catching an actual a11y bug instead of just finding text on the page.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What does userEvent give you that fireEvent does not?",
      a:`<p><code>fireEvent</code> dispatches a single synthetic DOM event directly. <code>userEvent</code> simulates the full sequence of events a real user interaction actually produces.</p>
      <pre>// fireEvent — one synthetic event, nothing else
fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: 'hello' } });

// userEvent — the realistic sequence a browser would fire
const user = userEvent.setup();
await user.type(input, 'hello');
// dispatches: focus → keydown → keypress → input → keyup, per character</pre>
      <p>For example, a real click fires <code>pointerdown</code>, <code>mousedown</code>, <code>pointerup</code>, <code>mouseup</code>, then <code>click</code> in order. <code>fireEvent.click</code> skips straight to firing <code>click</code> alone. That gap matters for components relying on focus management, hover state, or keyboard event handlers that <code>fireEvent</code>'s shortcut never triggers — <code>userEvent</code> catches bugs that <code>fireEvent</code> tests miss entirely.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Should you ever still use fireEvent?</strong> It's fine for firing low-level, one-off DOM events that don't correspond to a real user gesture (like a raw <code>scroll</code> or <code>resize</code> event) — for anything a user does with mouse or keyboard, <code>userEvent</code> is the better default.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"Spot the bugs: what's wrong with this RTL test, and how would you fix it?",
      a:`<pre>test('user can submit form', () => {
  render(<LoginForm onSubmit={jest.fn()} />);
  const emailInput = screen.getByLabelText('Email');
  const submitButton = screen.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i });

  fireEvent.change(emailInput, { target: { value: 'test@example.com' } });
  fireEvent.click(submitButton);

  expect(emailInput.value).toBe('test@example.com');
});</pre>
      <p>This test has five separate problems, all common enough to show up in real code review:</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Wrong target element.</strong> If the label isn't correctly associated with the input, <code>getByLabelText('Email')</code> can resolve to the <code><label></code> itself rather than the <code><input></code>, and firing a change event on a label does nothing.</li>
        <li><strong>fireEvent instead of userEvent.</strong> <code>fireEvent.change</code>/<code>fireEvent.click</code> bypass the realistic browser event sequence — prefer <code>await userEvent.type(...)</code> and <code>await userEvent.click(...)</code>.</li>
        <li><strong>No <code>await</code> on async work.</strong> If <code>onSubmit</code> is async or triggers a state update, the test doesn't wait for it to settle before asserting — needs <code>await</code>, and <code>waitFor</code> if the assertion depends on something appearing later.</li>
        <li><strong>Asserting the wrong thing.</strong> Checking that the input still holds the value you just typed proves almost nothing. The test should verify <code>expect(onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)</code> — that the callback actually fired with the right data.</li>
        <li><strong>No verification of the actual side effect.</strong> The test never checks that submission produced a visible result (a success message, a cleared loading state) — always assert on the post-submission UI, not just that a function was called.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Rewrite it correctly — what would the fixed version look like?</strong> Use <code>userEvent</code> to type into the input found via <code>getByRole('textbox', { name: /email/i })</code>, click submit the same way, then assert <code>expect(handleSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ email: 'test@example.com' }))</code> instead of reading the input's DOM value.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"In React Testing Library, what is the difference between getBy, findBy and queryBy?",
      a:`<table class="cmp">
<tr><th>Variant</th><th>Behaviour</th><th>Use it for</th></tr>
<tr><td><code>getBy*</code></td><td>Synchronous. Returns the element or <strong>throws</strong> if none (or more than one) matches.</td><td>Asserting something is on screen right now.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>queryBy*</code></td><td>Synchronous. Returns the element or <strong><code>null</code></strong>; does not throw when missing.</td><td>Asserting something is <em>absent</em>: <code>expect(screen.queryByText('Error')).not.toBeInTheDocument()</code>.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>findBy*</code></td><td>Asynchronous. Returns a promise that resolves when the element appears (default timeout 1000 ms), rejects otherwise.</td><td>Waiting for something that appears after async work (fetch, timers, state updates).</td></tr>
</table>
<ul>
<li>There are <code>All</code> variants (<code>getAllBy*</code>, <code>findAllBy*</code>, <code>queryAllBy*</code>) for multiple matches.</li>
<li><code>findBy*</code> is <code>getBy*</code> wrapped in <code>waitFor</code>, so you rarely need <code>waitFor</code> for a simple appearance.</li>
<li>Do not use <code>getBy*</code> to assert absence (it throws) or <code>queryBy*</code> to assert presence (you lose the helpful error message).</li>
</ul>
<pre>render(<UserCard id="1" />);
expect(screen.getByText(/loading/i)).toBeInTheDocument();          // there now
const name = await screen.findByRole('heading', { name: 'Jane Doe' }); // appears later
expect(screen.queryByText(/loading/i)).not.toBeInTheDocument();     // gone</pre>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is the difference between act() and waitFor() in React Testing Library?",
      a:`<ul>
<li><strong><code>act()</code></strong> makes sure all React updates triggered inside it (state changes, effects, scheduled work) are flushed before you make assertions. RTL wraps its render, <code>userEvent</code> and <code>fireEvent</code> calls in <code>act</code> for you, so you rarely call it by hand. The "not wrapped in act(...)" warning usually means a state update happened outside a tracked event, typically async work that finished after the test moved on.</li>
<li><strong><code>waitFor(callback)</code></strong> repeatedly runs a callback (polling plus a <code>MutationObserver</code>) until it stops throwing or a timeout is reached. Use it when the UI reaches the expected state <em>eventually</em>. Async queries (<code>findBy*</code>) already use it.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Rules of thumb:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Prefer <code>await screen.findBy...</code> for "appears later".</li>
<li>Put <strong>one assertion or a related group</strong> inside <code>waitFor</code>, and never side effects (like a click), because the callback can run many times.</li>
<li>Do not wrap <code>userEvent</code> calls in <code>act</code>; <code>await user.click(...)</code> is enough.</li>
<li>Do not use fixed <code>setTimeout</code> waits; they are slow and flaky.</li>
<li>Use <code>renderHook</code> and <code>act</code> together for testing custom hooks whose state changes are triggered from the test.</li>
</ul>
<pre>const user = userEvent.setup();
render(<SearchBox />);
await user.type(screen.getByRole('searchbox'), 'shoes');
await waitFor(() => expect(mockSearch).toHaveBeenCalledWith('shoes'));   // eventually true
expect(await screen.findByText('12 results')).toBeInTheDocument();</pre>`
    }
  ]
},

    {
      q:"How do you write an integration test for an API route with Supertest?",
      a:`<p>Integration tests verify that routing, middleware, validation, and the database all work together correctly — closer to what a real client experiences than a unit test of a single function.</p>
<pre><code>import request from 'supertest';

import { db } from '../db';

  });

<p>Test the API contract, not internal implementation details. Use a real (test) database rather than mocking the DB layer — an integration test that mocks the database isn't really testing integration.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"Mock vs Stub vs Spy — what's the difference?",
      a:`<p>All three are "test doubles," but they answer different questions about the code under test.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Stub:</strong> replaces a function with a fake that returns hardcoded values. You don't care how it was called — you just need controlled, predictable output. <code>jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(data)</code></li>
<li><strong>Spy:</strong> wraps the real function, lets it actually execute, but records how it was called so you can assert on that afterward while keeping real behavior. <code>jest.spyOn(obj, 'method')</code></li>
<li><strong>Mock:</strong> pre-programs expectations up front; the test fails if the function isn't called exactly as specified. Stricter than a spy. <code>jest.fn().mockImplementation(...)</code></li>
</ul>
<pre><code>// Stub an external service
jest.mock('../services/email');
sendEmail.mockResolvedValue({ success: true });

// Spy on a real method, then restore it
const spy = jest.spyOn(logger, 'error');
await handleRequest(badRequest);
expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Validation failed', expect.any(Object));
spy.mockRestore();

// Mock with sequenced return values
const mockDb = jest.fn()
  .mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 1 })
  .mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 2 })
  .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('DB down'));</code></pre>
<p>Rule of thumb: stub when you only care about output, spy when you want real behavior plus verification, mock when the interaction itself (that a call happened, with what args, how many times) is the thing under test.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is the 'Testing Trophy,' and how does it change what you test?",
      a:`<p>Kent C. Dodds's Testing Trophy reprioritizes the classic testing pyramid: instead of "mostly unit tests," it weights integration tests as the biggest layer, because they give the best confidence-to-cost ratio for a typical UI app.</p>
<div class="diagram" data-sd="testing-3"><svg viewBox="0 0 800 240" width="800" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Testing trophy: static, unit, integration (largest), end-to-end">
<polygon points="330,20 470,20 450,58 350,58" fill="var(--gold-soft)" stroke="var(--gold)"/><text x="400" y="44" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11" fill="var(--text)" font-weight="600">E2E</text>
<polygon points="300,62 500,62 520,142 280,142" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="400" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" fill="var(--text)" font-weight="600">Integration</text>
<polygon points="330,146 470,146 460,178 340,178" fill="var(--panel)" stroke="var(--border)"/><text x="400" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11" fill="var(--text)" font-weight="600">Unit</text>
<rect x="290" y="184" width="220" height="30" rx="6" fill="var(--panel-2)" stroke="var(--border)"/><text x="400" y="204" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--text)">Static: TypeScript, ESLint</text>
<text x="540" y="42"  font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10" fill="var(--muted)">Playwright: a few critical user journeys</text>
<text x="540" y="100"  font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10" fill="var(--muted)">RTL + MSW, Supertest + real DB container:</text><text x="540" y="114"  font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10" fill="var(--accent)">most confidence per unit of effort</text>
<text x="540" y="166"  font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10" fill="var(--muted)">pure logic, reducers, utils</text>
<text x="540" y="202"  font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10" fill="var(--muted)">catches typos and type errors for free</text>
<text x="10" y="100"  font-family="var(--sans)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--text)">The more your tests</text><text x="10" y="116"  font-family="var(--sans)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--text)">resemble real use,</text><text x="10" y="132"  font-family="var(--sans)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--text)">the more confidence</text><text x="10" y="148"  font-family="var(--sans)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--text)">they give you.</text>
</svg></div>

<ul>
<li><strong>Static analysis (base):</strong> TypeScript + ESLint catch a whole class of bugs before a test even runs — zero cost, ongoing payoff.</li>
<li><strong>Unit tests:</strong> pure functions, reducers, utilities. Fast and isolated, but low confidence about how real user flows behave.</li>
<li><strong>Integration tests (the largest slice):</strong> components rendered with their children, hooks, and mocked network calls — this is what most React Testing Library tests are. Best confidence-to-cost ratio.</li>
<li><strong>E2E (top, smallest slice):</strong> Playwright/Cypress driving a real browser through full user flows. High confidence, but slow and more prone to flakiness — reserve it for critical paths like login, checkout, and signup.</li>
</ul>
<p>The interview-ready version: don't chase 100% coverage — focus on testing user-observable behavior at the integration level, with a thin layer of E2E on top for the paths that would hurt most in production.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What typically causes flaky frontend tests, and how do you eliminate them?",
      a:`<ul>
<li><strong>Use auto-waiting queries/locators:</strong> React Testing Library's <code>findBy*</code>, and Playwright/Cypress locators, retry automatically — avoid a manual <code>sleep()</code>/fixed <code>wait()</code>, which is either too short (flaky) or too long (slow).</li>
<li><strong>Deterministic data:</strong> seed fixtures rather than depending on shared or production data that can change between runs.</li>
<li><strong>Mock time:</strong> anything time-based should use <code>jest.useFakeTimers()</code> (or an E2E framework's clock API) instead of real timers racing the test.</li>
<li><strong>Isolate tests:</strong> each test sets up and tears down its own state — one test's leftover state should never leak into the next.</li>
<li><strong>Mock the network:</strong> MSW gives deterministic responses; a real network call is a source of nondeterminism you don't need in a unit/integration test.</li>
<li><strong>Retry once, fix always:</strong> a CI retry can absorb a one-off flake, but track the flake rate per test and treat a rising rate as a bug to fix, not noise to suppress.</li>
</ul>`

// Predict the output. A card shows a snippet and an empty <div class="predict">. The reader types what the

function predictFormat(value, nested){

  if(t === 'function') return value.name ? '[Function: ' + value.name + ']' : '[Function (anonymous)]';

  if(Array.isArray(value)) return value.length ? '[ ' + value.map(function(x){ return predictFormat(x, true); }).join(', ') + ' ]' : '[]';

    "const __console = { log: (...a) => __send(a.map((x) => predictFormat(x, false)).join(' ')) };\n" +
    "const __err = (e, prefix) => __send(prefix + ' ' + (e && e.name ? e.name + ': ' + e.message : String(e)));\n" +
    "if (typeof process !== 'undefined' && process.on) {\n" +
    "  process.on('uncaughtException', (e) => __err(e, 'Uncaught'));\n" +

    "  addEventListener('unhandledrejection', (ev) => { if (ev.preventDefault) ev.preventDefault(); __err(ev.reason, 'Uncaught (in promise)'); });\n" +
    "}\n" +
    "try { (function (console) {\n'use strict';\n" + code + "\n})(__console); } catch (e) { __err(e, 'Uncaught'); }\n" +

// Compares what the reader said with what it printed, line by line, judging the answer and not the spacing.
function predictCompare(predicted, actual){
  const said = String(predicted).split('\n');

  while(said.length && !said[0].trim()) said.shift();
  const norm = function(s){ return s.replace(/\s+/g, '').replace(/[“”‘’"]/g, "'"); };
  const same = function(a, b){
    const x = norm(a), y = norm(b);
    if(x === y) return true;
    // a bare string written with quotes ("a" for a) is forgiven; a string written as a number is not
    return x.length > 2 && x[0] === "'" && x[x.length - 1] === "'" && x.indexOf("'", 1) === x.length - 1 && y.indexOf("'") < 0 && x.slice(1, -1) === y;
  };
  const n = Math.max(said.length, actual.length);
  const rows = [];
  let right = 0;
  for(let i = 0; i < n; i++){
    const s = i < said.length ? said[i] : '', p = i < actual.length ? actual[i] : '';
    const ok = i < said.length && i < actual.length && same(s, p);
    if(ok) right++;
    rows.push({ said: s, printed: p, ok: ok });

// Listen mode: read a section's questions and answers aloud with the device's own voice (speech synthesis).
// Nothing is generated or downloaded. Code, tables and diagrams are replaced by a short spoken marker.
function speakText(html){
  let s = String(html).replace(/<!--x:extras-->[\s\S]*?<!--\/x:extras-->/g, ' ');
  s = s.replace(/<summary[\s\S]*?<\/summary>/g, ' ')
    .replace(/<details class="reveal">/g, ' The answer. ')
    .replace(/<pre[\s\S]*?<\/pre>/g, ' Code example on the card. ')
    .replace(/<svg[\s\S]*?<\/svg>/g, ' Diagram on the card. ')
    .replace(/<table[\s\S]*?<\/table>/g, ' Table on the card. ')
    .replace(/<\/?(?:p|li|ul|ol|div|br|h[1-6]|tr|td|th|blockquote)[^>]*>/gi, ' ')   // block tags break the text, inline ones do not
    .replace(/<[^>]+>/g, '');
  s = s.replace(/&#x([0-9a-f]+);/gi, function(m, h){ return String.fromCodePoint(parseInt(h, 16)); })
    .replace(/&#(\d+);/g, function(m, d){ return String.fromCodePoint(Number(d)); })
    .replace(/ /g, ' ').replace(/—/g, '—').replace(/→/g, '→').replace(/</g, '<').replace(/>/g, '>').replace(/&/g, '&');

// Some browsers stop a long utterance after about 15 seconds, so speak short chunks.
function speakChunks(text, max){
